questions.q: State the five postulates of the Kinetic Molecular Theory of ideal gases. For each postulate, identify which macroscopic gas property (pressure, temperature, volume, diffusion rate) it primarily explains.
questions.a: The five postulates: (1) Gases consist of large number of tiny particles (molecules) with negligible volume compared to container volume — explains compressibility and Boyle's Law. (2) Particles are in constant random straight-line motion — explains diffusion (Graham's Law) and pressure. (3) Collisions are perfectly elastic (no net KE loss) — explains pressure maintenance and Charles's Law. (4) No intermolecular forces except during collisions — explains ideal gas equation applicability and lack of condensation at high T. (5) Average KE ∝ absolute temperature (KE_avg = 3/2 kT) — explains temperature-pressure-volume relationships. A wrong answer revealing confusion between "negligible volume" (postulate 1) and "no forces" (postulate 4) shows the student cannot distinguish excluded volume effects from attractive force effects — a critical error for real gas deviations later.

questions.q: A student argues: "Since gas molecules move at ~500 m/s at room temperature, a perfume molecule should cross a 5 m room in 0.01 s. But we smell it after minutes. Therefore KMT is wrong." Identify the flaw in this reasoning using KMT postulates and the concept of mean free path.
questions.a: The flaw: the student assumes straight-line uninterrupted motion (postulate 2) but ignores collisions. In reality, a molecule undergoes ~10⁹ collisions per second at STP. Mean free path λ = kT/(√2 π d² P) ≈ 68 nm for air at STP. The molecule follows a random walk: net displacement ∝ √(number of steps) × λ. For 5 m displacement, time ≈ (5 m)² / (λ × u_avg) ≈ minutes. A wrong answer citing "air resistance" or "gravity" shows the student doesn't grasp that KMT already accounts for collisions via postulate 3 (elastic collisions) and that diffusion is a statistical process, not ballistic.

questions.q: Derive the kinetic gas equation P = (1/3) ρ u²_rms starting from a single molecule of mass m moving with velocity components (u_x, u_y, u_z) in a cubic container of side L. Show all steps including the assumption of isotropy.
questions.a: Step 1: Momentum change per collision with wall perpendicular to x-axis = 2mu_x. Step 2: Time between collisions with same wall = 2L/u_x. Step 3: Force from one molecule = Δp/Δt = mu_x²/L. Step 4: Pressure from one molecule = F/A = mu_x²/L³ = mu_x²/V. Step 5: For N molecules, P = (Nm/V) × (u_x²)_avg. Step 6: By isotropy, (u_x²)_avg = (u_y²)_avg = (u_z²)_avg = ⅓ u²_rms. Step 7: P = (1/3)(Nm/V)u²_rms = (1/3)ρ u²_rms. A wrong answer skipping step 6 (isotropy) or using u_avg instead of u_rms reveals confusion between vector components and scalar speed — a common board exam error where students write P = (1/3)ρ u²_avg and lose marks.

questions.q: Compare the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution curves for (a) O₂ at 300 K and 600 K, (b) H₂ and O₂ at 300 K. For each case, state how the peak position (u_mp), peak height, and area under curve change, and justify using the formula u_mp = √(2RT/M).
questions.a: (a) O₂ at 300 K vs 600 K: u_mp increases by √2 (since u_mp ∝ √T). Peak height decreases (area constant = 1, curve broadens). Area under curve remains 1 (probability normalization). (b) H₂ vs O₂ at 300 K: M_H₂ = 2, M_O₂ = 32 → u_mp(H₂) = 4 × u_mp(O₂). H₂ peak shifts right, becomes lower and broader. Area = 1 for both. A wrong answer saying "area increases with temperature" reveals the student treats the curve as a histogram of molecule counts rather than a probability density function — a fundamental misunderstanding of statistical mechanics.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "At the same temperature, all gas molecules have the same kinetic energy, so they must have the same speed." Provide a counterexample using N₂ (M=28) and He (M=4) at 300 K, calculating u_rms for each.
questions.a: The statement is false. KE_avg = 3/2 kT per molecule is the same, but KE = ½ mu²_rms → u_rms = √(3RT/M). For N₂: u_rms = √(3×8.314×300/0.028) = 517 m/s. For He: u_rms = √(3×8.314×300/0.004) = 1368 m/s. He moves 2.65× faster despite same KE. A wrong answer claiming "same KE means same speed" confuses kinetic energy (scalar, depends on v²) with velocity (vector) — a persistent misconception from Class 9 physics where KE = ½mv² is taught without emphasizing the mass dependence of speed for fixed KE.

questions.q: Design a thought experiment to measure the root mean square speed of nitrogen molecules at 300 K using only a pressure gauge, a thermometer, a known volume container, and the ideal gas equation. Write the step-by-step procedure and the final formula you would use.
questions.a: Procedure: (1) Fill rigid container of known volume V with N₂ gas. (2) Measure pressure P at temperature T using gauge and thermometer. (3) Calculate density ρ = PM/RT from ideal gas equation (M = 0.028 kg/mol for N₂). (4) Use kinetic gas equation P = ⅓ ρ u²_rms → u_rms = √(3P/ρ) = √(3RT/M). (5) Plug in R=8.314, T=300, M=0.028 → u_rms = 517 m/s. A poor answer suggesting "track a single molecule" or "use speed camera" reveals inability to connect macroscopic measurable quantities (P, V, T) to microscopic properties — the central bridge KMT provides. This also tests if the student recognizes that u_rms is derivable without direct speed measurement.
